clinicalPearls: Sudden-onset itchy weals, angio-oedema, or both, lasting less than six weeks
Individual weals are transient, each resolving within a day without leaving a mark
Common triggers include viral infection, foods, drugs and insect stings, though many cases are idiopathic
When accompanied by airway, breathing or circulatory compromise it may be part of anaphylaxis and needs adrenaline
It is largely a clinical diagnosis, and extensive investigation is usually unnecessary
Non-sedating antihistamines are first-line, with a short corticosteroid course for severe flares
reference.pathophysiology: Acute urticaria results from activation and degranulation of cutaneous mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine and other mediators that cause vasodilatation, increased vascular permeability (producing weals and angio-oedema) and pruritus. Degranulation may be immunological, classically IgE-mediated in allergy, or non-immunological through direct mast-cell activation by drugs, infections or other stimuli. The transient nature of individual weals reflects the short-lived local mediator response.
additionalDifferentials: Urticarial vasculitis (weals lasting more than a day, leaving bruising)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the history and transient weals
Assessment for anaphylaxis features requiring immediate treatment
Targeted allergy evaluation only where a specific trigger is suspected
Consideration of urticarial vasculitis if weals persist or bruise
Limited testing, as most acute cases are self-limiting
redFlags: Airway compromise, wheeze or hypotension indicating anaphylaxis
Angio-oedema of the tongue or throat
Weals lasting more than a day or leaving bruising (urticarial vasculitis)
reference.prognosis: Acute urticaria is usually self-limiting, resolving within days to a few weeks; a minority evolve into chronic urticaria.
pitfalls: Missing evolving anaphylaxis in a patient with urticaria
Overlooking bradykinin-mediated angio-oedema, which does not respond to antihistamines
management: Identify and remove the precipitant where one is apparent, such as a culprit drug, food or infection
Give a second-generation non-sedating H1 antihistamine as first-line treatment, up-dosing within recommended limits if the response is inadequate
Add a short course of oral corticosteroid for severe or extensive flares
Recognise accompanying anaphylaxis and treat immediately with intramuscular adrenaline and supportive resuscitation
Reassure that the condition is usually self-limiting and avoid extensive investigation in typical cases
Reassess and refer to allergy or dermatology if weals persist beyond six weeks or if painful, bruising or long-lasting lesions suggest urticarial vasculitis
